Measured

318 apps fit inside one photo.

A complete 2D game you can actually play, a Breakout with a paddle, bricks, lives and a win, is 13 KB. Not 13 megabytes, and the same file runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux. It is that small because nothing is bundled inside it that your computer already has.

Every measurement, how it was taken, and what still does not work →

* Sustained compute. The same program built twice, native and as a Krate app, finished 300 million calculations in the same time, and produced identical output. Short tasks are the worst case: a program that does almost nothing but ask the system for things runs about 5× slower, because a fixed 6 ms startup is most of its total.

* Both measured on the same Mac with du -sk: Discord is 431 MB, and the 2D game above, a playable Breakout, is 13,161 bytes for all three operating systems together. Discord is the comparison because it solves the same problem Krate solves, one codebase shipped to Mac, Windows and Linux, and it does it by putting a copy of a web browser inside the app. So does VS Code at 1.4 GB, which is 117,000 times the game. A chat client does far more than a game; the number that matters is the floor each approach starts from, which is a browser for one and nothing for the other. Krate itself is a 17.5 MB install, once, shared by every app you run.

Measured on an Apple Silicon Mac. Windows and Linux are not measured yet. Full numbers, methodology, and what we have not tested.

See it work

One word to start.

Making an app, opening one someone sent you, and putting one on Krate Cloud.

krate / product walkthrough

See the product

A real app, from request to reopen.

This demo creates a Krate app, opens it, checks its requested access, saves local data, and opens it again.

It's just an app

You get a real app. It opens a window, keeps your settings, saves your things in its own database, remembers your sign-in, and can send you a notification or open a link.

What it cannot do is help itself. Before it opens, Krate shows you what it wants, in plain words rather than permissions jargon, and it gets only what you allow. An app that keeps a list never sees your folders.

The same file works on Mac, Windows, and Linux. Not three downloads. One.

Start here

Install once. Open anything.

You install the runtime once. After that, you can open any .krate app someone sends you. Double-click it, or run it from a terminal. That is the whole idea.

macOS or Linux — paste into a terminal

curl -fsSL https://krate.tech/install.sh | sh

Windows — paste into PowerShell

irm https://krate.tech/install.ps1 | iex

That is the only install. You never do it again per app.

Hit a snag? Common issues & fixes
  • A new terminal says krate: command not found or 'krate' is not recognized. The install folder is not on your PATH yet. Open a fresh terminal, or add the PATH line the installer printed at the end.
  • An app won't open: a matching implementation was not found in the linker. The app needs a newer Krate than you have. Update by running the install command above again.
  • Making an app, the Rust install failed: could not amend shell profile ... Permission denied. This is fixed in a newer Krate. Run the install command above again to update.
  • I ran ./krate and it said no such file. After installing, the command is just krate, with no ./. Use krate run app.krate.
  • Double-clicking a .krate does nothing. Reinstall with the latest version, which sets up the file association so double-click opens it.

Still stuck? Tell us → report it on GitHub. The same list, and where to report, is one command away in the terminal: krate doctor shows your setup and where to get help.

What works today

The useful parts are already real.

Krate is early, but the core product journey works now and is built in public.

One file, three systems

The same .krate app opens on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

Build it by talking

Run krate mcp once to connect Krate to Claude Desktop or Cursor. Then ask for an app in plain words and it gets built, checked, and handed back as a file.

Five AI tools, your pick

Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini, GitHub Copilot, or xAI Grok. krate ai shows which ones you already have.

It says no when it must

Ask for something Krate cannot do and you get a straight answer in about a second, not a broken app twenty minutes later.

Clear requested access

The app carries the access it requests. Krate shows it before the app runs and enforces the user’s choice.

Local app behavior

Windowed apps can save locally, keep their state, and reopen later.

Opens in 16 milliseconds

Median cold start on an Apple Silicon Mac. A single frame of 60 fps video is 16.7 ms, so most Krate apps are open before your screen finishes drawing one.

The sandbox is free

300 million operations: 703.9 ms native, 706.3 ms in Krate. Sandboxed code at native speed, with the output checked identical before every timing.

2D games run here

A Breakout you play with the arrow keys, in a 13 KB file that opens on all three systems.

Proof by pixels

Real apps, each shown as a real screenshot.

Every image is the actual window the runtime drew, captured on one command. The arcade game up top is a 15.9 KB file that runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

Each was checked with krate run app.wasm --shoot frame.png. The runtime paints the window to an image on any machine, no display needed, so you can check one yourself.

What is tested and working

Here is what runs today, and how to check it yourself.

Every app below was built and its window was rendered to an image and looked at. No mockups.

Apps that run today

Calculator, temperature converter, notes, a 500-row scrolling list, a persistence counter that saves and reloads, HTTP fetch, real-time animation, tabbed settings with a slider, switch, and progress bar, a file tree, a stats dashboard with a bar chart beside the widgets, a weather card, a Pomodoro timer, a world clock, a contacts book backed by SQLite, a 3D scene, and a 2D arcade shooter you play with the arrow keys. Twenty-seven example apps ship in apps/krate-*, ten are published on Krate Cloud, and nine are shown as screenshots above.

Check one yourself

Run any app and have the runtime paint its window to a PNG, on any machine, no display needed:

krate run app.wasm --shoot frame.png

Then open frame.png. If the app drew a window, you will see it. This shipped in v0.1.0, the current release.

Not ready yet

Most of the surface works today, including database storage (store.sql) and pushing your own pixels into an image widget (ui.image) -- a real SQL budgeting app and an image viewer are among the apps that build and run. The one gap: clipboard works on Mac and Linux (and headless), but the Windows clipboard is not wired up yet.

Where it runs

Six builds. Both chips. All three systems.

Every release publishes each of these, and the same app file opens on all of them.

Shipping now

  • macOS on Apple Silicon tested
  • macOS on Intel
  • Windows on Intel and AMD
  • Windows on ARM tested
  • Linux on Intel and AMD
  • Linux on ARM

Windows on ARM covers a Windows VM on an Apple Silicon Mac, which is how most people try Windows without owning a Windows machine. Linux on ARM covers a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 and most cloud ARM instances. Marked tested where a person has installed and run it, rather than only built it.

Next

  • Speech on ARM builds. Everything else works there today; transcription needs a newer C++ toolchain than those build containers carry.
  • A signed installer for Windows and macOS, so neither system warns about an unknown developer.
  • Linux on RISC-V, once there is somebody asking for it.
  • Phones and tablets. The runtime is portable and the window layer is not. Real work, not a recompile.
  • The browser. Krate apps are already WebAssembly, so this is the shortest path of the four and the one that would let somebody try an app without installing anything at all.

Krate Cloud

Apps you can look at before you trust them. Every listing is read out of the file itself: its size, its identity, and every permission it asks for, so nobody describes their own app more kindly than it behaves.

Publishing goes through Krate Cloud. Running does not: apps open on your own computer, with exactly the access you allow.

Questions people asked

Direct answers about Krate.

These questions came from developers seeing Krate for the first time. The short answer is first, with the technical boundary underneath it.

04 / AIHow does Krate make an AI-created app safer?

AI-generated code receives no special trust. During authoring, Krate rejects an app if it imports system interfaces outside the Krate capability boundary. At runtime, the app begins without access to the user’s files or network.

The app requests specific capabilities, the user reviews them, and the runtime enforces the decision before approved host operations happen. This limits what the app can reach. It does not prove that the app is bug-free.

08 / TodayWhat can Krate apps do today, and can it convert my existing app?

Today Krate runs a real range of small apps that fit its current UI and capability set: a calculator, a temperature converter, notes and lists, tabbed settings with sliders, switches, and progress bars, a file tree, a stats dashboard with a bar chart, a weather card, a Pomodoro timer, a world clock, real-time animation, a 3D scene, a 2D arcade shooter you play with the arrow keys, HTTP fetch, local persistence, database-backed apps on SQLite, and portable command-line tools. Twenty-seven example apps ship in the repository, and ten are published on Krate Cloud. The one gap left: clipboard works on Mac and Linux, but the Windows clipboard is not wired up yet.

It does not automatically convert an existing Swift, Electron, Tauri, or native application yet. Current apps must use Krate APIs. AI-assisted porting is a planned development target, and it will reimplement supported behavior rather than pretend an incompatible binary became portable.

09 / CloudDoes Krate Cloud run the app on someone else’s server?

No. Krate Cloud is the publishing and distribution layer: it hands you a file, and it does not run it. Signing and updates are not built yet.

The app still opens through the Krate runtime on your own computer, where you review and control local access. You can browse what people have published at krate.tech/cloud, and publish your own with krate publish or from the publish page.

About

Who is building this.

Krate is built by Yashraj Pardeshi, its founder and builder. He has been building it solo since April 2026, in public, from Singapore.

The problem it answers has not been solved: software still cannot move between computers the way a file can, and you cannot tell what a program does before you run it. Krate is one answer to both: a single app file that opens on Mac, Windows, and Linux, and carries the list of what it is allowed to do on the outside, where you can read it before anything runs.

Every claim here is checkable. Machines he has never touched open the app, type into it, and photograph the result on every push; the evidence is in the build logs. It is early, and the limits are published alongside the product.

More at incyashraj.github.io and GitHub.
